title: The afterlife of gadgets
text: The world now throws away over sixty million tonnes of {{1}} (ELECTRON) waste every year, and the total is growing five times faster than recycling capacity. Barely a fifth is {{2}} (FORM) documented and recycled. Much of the rest disappears into drawers, landfill and informal scrapyards, where circuit boards are burnt in the open, {{3}} (POISON) soil, water and lungs. The absurdity is that this refuse is rich: the {{4}} (CONCENTRATE) of gold, silver and palladium in a tonne of discarded phones exceeds that of the ore those metals are usually mined from. Urban mining has therefore moved from slogan to serious {{5}} (PROPOSE), with facilities designed to recover metals from circuitry at industrial scale. Japan supplied the showcase: the medals awarded at the Tokyo Olympics were {{6}} (FASHION) entirely from gold, silver and bronze reclaimed from donated devices. Design, as ever, is decisive — batteries soldered into place and screens glued shut make component {{7}} (RECOVER) slow and expensive — and regulators have begun {{8}} (DEMAND) repairability scores and spare-part guarantees, to which manufacturers, grumbling, are adjusting. Until then, the drawer of dead phones in most homes remains what it has always been: an unvisited, ever-growing mine.

gaps.explanation: 'burnt in the open, poisoning soil' — participle clause of result.
'the concentration of gold in old phones' — noun from concentrate.
'from slogan to serious proposal' — noun from propose.
'were fashioned from reclaimed devices' — passive participle: made, from fashion (verb).
'make component recovery slow' — noun from recover.
'have begun demanding repairability scores' — gerund from demand.
